quizzes.question: Your agent has finished building a login page you approved. Which video do you watch next?
quizzes.questionMore: A login page: you watched its plan video and approved it, and the agent has built it.

options.label: The plan video, revised
options.why: The plan video is made before any code; once you approve it, it isn't shown again for the build.

options.label: The walkthrough video: the page running
options.why: Right: after the build, the walkthrough video shows the change running, and you review it.

options.label: The system video
options.why: The system video is brought up to date last, after you review the walkthrough video.

quizzes.explain: After the build comes the walkthrough video: it shows the change running, and you review it before the system video catches up.
quizzes.walkMeThrough: The plan video came first, before any code, and you approved it. Now the agent has built the login page. The next video in the loop is the walkthrough video: the page running, which you review. Only after that is the system video brought up to date.

quizzes.question: On a new laptop, you've run the first three install commands: the tooling, setup and the skill. In a second repo, what still has to run?
quizzes.questionMore: Same laptop, a different project: the tooling, setup and the skill are already on it.

options.label: All four commands again
options.why: Three of the four are once per machine: the laptop already has them.

options.label: Only `reel init`, which your agent can run
options.why: Right: only `reel init` is per repo, and the agent runs it when you first plan there.

options.label: `setup` again, then `reel init`
options.why: setup is once per machine; it already ran on this laptop.

quizzes.explain: The tooling, setup and the skill are once per machine; each repo only needs `reel init`, and your agent runs it for you.
quizzes.walkMeThrough: The npm install, setup and the skill went onto the laptop once, and every repo on it uses them. The second repo has no `.reelplanning/` folder yet. So only `reel init` runs there, and your agent runs it for you the first time you plan.

quizzes.question: In another plan's video, fresh eyes flag the phrase “stage map”, and its author thinks it's clear. What happens before the review page opens?
quizzes.questionMore: Fresh eyes looked at another plan's video, and the newcomer couldn't follow “stage map”.

options.label: Nothing: it opens as it is
options.why: A finding left unanswered stops the build, so the page can't open as it is.

options.label: The author answers it: fixed, a meaning, or kept with the reason
options.why: Right: the author answers every finding, and keeping it needs a reason.

options.label: The build waits for you to decide
options.why: The author answers fresh eyes before you see the video; you aren't asked.

quizzes.explain: Every finding is answered before the page opens, fixed, given a meaning, or kept with the reason; the build won't pass one left unanswered.
quizzes.walkMeThrough: Fresh eyes found “stage map” hard to follow in that video. The author may disagree, but can't ignore it. They answer it under the finding: fix the line, give the phrase a meaning you can click, or keep it and say why. Only then does the build pass and the page open.

quizzes.question: You pause on a scene with a table, and move your pointer over it. How do you know the table leads to the guide?
quizzes.questionMore: The scene is paused, and the table is the thing it's about.

options.label: A black tab is drawn on it
options.why: Nothing heavy is drawn on the video: no tab, only a ring and a small label on hover.

options.label: A thin ring, and “More in the guide”
options.why: Right: on hover, a thin ring and “More in the guide”; a click on that label opens it.

options.label: Nothing: you open Terms
options.why: Terms says what words mean; the table shows its own way into the guide.

quizzes.explain: A thing that leads to the guide stays quiet: a faint arrow when paused, and on hover a thin ring and “More in the guide”.
quizzes.walkMeThrough: The video is paused, so the table shows a faint arrow. Your pointer moves over it, and a thin ring and a small grey “More in the guide” appear. Click that label, and the guide opens at the table's part.

quizzes.question: In a repo set up for Claude Code (`reel init --agent claude`), you press Send at 11 pm, and no agent session is open. What happens to your review?
quizzes.questionMore: Your agent's chat is closed for the night; the review server is still running, and the repo's config names `claude` as its agent.

options.label: It's lost
options.why: Nothing is lost: the review server keeps it in the inbox first.

options.label: It waits for your next session
options.why: It waits for your next session only in a repo set up with `--agent none`, which has no command to start; here the headless run starts.

options.label: The headless run starts on it, in the sandbox
options.why: Right: no session is waiting, so the headless run starts, inside the sandbox.

quizzes.explain: With no session waiting, the review server starts the headless run on it, inside the sandbox.
quizzes.walkMeThrough: The review server keeps your review in the inbox, then hands it on once. No session is waiting at eleven at night. So the server starts the headless run, your agent on its own, inside the sandbox, and it works on your review.

quizzes.question: In step 6, the agent made three choices: one labelled visible, one labelled close, one with no label; no late fixes lately. Which of them pause the walkthrough video?
quizzes.questionMore: Step six of some plan, and the labels the agent gave its choices.

options.label: All three
options.why: Unlabelled choices never pause: they go on the list at the end.

options.label: Only the visible one
options.why: Right: only visible or hard-to-undo pause, with no late fix lately.

options.label: The visible and the close one
options.why: Close pauses only when a recent late fix shares its label; here there's none.

quizzes.explain: A choice labelled visible or hard-to-undo pauses; close and unlabelled choices go on the list at the end, unless a recent late fix shares their label.
quizzes.walkMeThrough: The visible choice changes what you see, so it pauses in the scene that runs it. The close one has no recent late fix sharing its label, so it goes on the list at the end. The unlabelled one goes on the list too. That's one pause.

quizzes.question: You accept a walkthrough that adds a new part, the scheduler, to the project's parts and its glossary. What happens to this video?
quizzes.questionMore: The scheduler is a new part, with a row in the glossary.

options.label: Nothing: it's a record
options.why: This video is kept current: a change to its three files names scenes to rebuild.

options.label: spec-diff names scenes to rebuild, and one explains the scheduler
options.why: Right: spec-diff names the scenes, and the new word gets a scene of its own.

options.label: It's made again from scratch
options.why: Only the scenes spec-diff names are rebuilt, not the whole video.

quizzes.explain: A change to those files makes spec-diff name the scenes to rebuild, and every word in the glossary gets a scene.
quizzes.walkMeThrough: The walkthrough was accepted, so the parts and the glossary now name the scheduler. spec-diff compares them with what this video covers and names the scenes to rebuild. And since every word in the glossary has a scene, one is added for the scheduler.

frames.title: A long plan
frames.narration: Your agent, the AI assistant that writes your code, hands you a plan like this: five steps, eight hundred lines, and four questions at the end. You can answer them right in the chat. But that's a lot to read, so it's easy to skim, and hard to see what each question is asking.

frames.title: A plan, as a video
frames.narration: reelplanning turns that plan into a short narrated video, which stops at each question for your answer. It's a row of scenes, each a picture and a line or two, grouped into chapters. The rest goes on a page under it, the guide.

frames.title: One loop for every change
frames.narration: Used in full, every change follows one loop. The plan video tells the plan, before any code, and your review's answers become decisions. The agent builds, noting each choice it makes alone. The walkthrough video shows it running, for your review too. Then the system video, this one, catches up.

frames.title: How much you use
frames.narration: You choose how much of it you use. The basic unit is one video: a plan video, or an explainer, a video of something already there. Add a walkthrough after the build, if you want, or take the whole pipeline: your answers kept as decisions, every review on record, and the system video kept current. From here on, this video shows the whole pipeline.

frames.title: The skill, and which agents
frames.narration: It all runs through the plan-to-video skill, the instructions your agent follows. It's tested with Claude Code, though not yet its sandboxed run on a normal machine. Codex has basic support.

frames.title: The tooling, once per machine
frames.narration: Installing takes four commands. First, once per machine, npm installs the tooling from GitHub. That adds `reelplanning`, and `reel`, the reel CLI, which keeps the project's record.

frames.title: What the videos need
frames.narration: Second, `reelplanning setup`, once per machine too, gets what videos need: a voice, a transcriber for captions, a browser that draws the frames, and HyperFrames' skills.

frames.title: The skill, into your agent
frames.narration: Third, `npx skills add` copies the plan-to-video skill from that install to where Claude Code, Codex and the other agents read skills.

frames.title: Then, in each repo
frames.narration: Last, in each repo, `reel init` writes `.reelplanning/`: the project's description, its parts and words, the decision log: every answer you give, and the command that starts your agent when a review arrives. Your agent runs it for you, and in a repo with code, fills in the description and parts from it.

frames.narration: Quick check: your agent has finished building a login page you approved. Which video do you watch next?

frames.title: The plan, in your repo
frames.narration: To start, type `/plan-to-video` in Claude Code, or `$plan-to-video` in Codex, or just ask your agent for a plan. From there, your agent runs the commands. It writes the plan into your repo as `plan.md`: a few steps, each with its cases, interface and an example, and a numbered question wherever the choice is yours.

frames.title: Held to what you decided
frames.narration: Then `reel check` holds the plan to what you decided: your answers on each part it touches are rules it must cite, or say why it replaces one.

frames.title: From plan to video
frames.narration: The agent writes a storyboard and the frames; `reelplanning build` voices it with a local voice, adds captions and checks every frame.

frames.title: Fresh eyes, before you
frames.narration: Before you see it, fresh eyes look: two new agents who know nothing of the plan. One lists what a newcomer couldn't follow; the other, what breaks the frame rules, like one reading order and each name on its thing. The author answers every finding: fixed, given a meaning, or kept with a reason.

frames.title: The review page
frames.narration: Your agent starts the review server, `reelplanning review`, and it keeps running after your session ends. It serves the review page, and a notification says when a video is ready: here, four choices to make and five quick checks, about five minutes.

frames.title: Quick check: a second repo
frames.question: On a new laptop, you've run the first three install commands: the tooling, setup and the skill. In a second repo, what still has to run?

`setup` again, then `reel init`

frames.narration: Quick check. On a new laptop, you've run the first three commands. So in a second repo: what still has to run?

frames.title: The review player
frames.narration: Open a video, and it plays in the review player, its chapters on the timeline. Draw on a frame, or comment anywhere, and it's tied to the plan step on screen.

frames.title: It stops, and you answer on the frame
frames.narration: At each question the video stops, and you click a card to answer; More on a card says what picking it means. Not ready? Explain this more asks for it again, explained better. None fits? Write your own words in the answer bar.

frames.title: Terms, Ask, and the plan text
frames.narration: Stuck on a word? Terms opens in the side panel. Ask about this, or Q, asks an agent about the scene. The Plan switch shows the plan text.

frames.title: A quick check, and why
frames.narration: Now and then, a quick check asks what the plan will do on a new case. Once you answer, each card says why. And Walk me through it works the case through.

frames.title: The guide, under the video
frames.narration: Scroll down, and the guide is under the video, which keeps playing small in the corner. It holds what a video can't: every case, the interface, worked examples, and diagrams to step through.

frames.title: A quiet way into the guide
frames.narration: A thing in a scene can lead to its part of the guide, quietly: a faint arrow when paused; on hover, a thin ring and More in the guide.

frames.title: A note on any words
frames.narration: On the guide, select any words to leave a note, suggest an edit, or ask. It goes with the same review.

frames.title: Finish: approve, or ask for changes
frames.narration: When you're done, press Finish. Approve, and the agent works your comments into the plan, with no new video. Request changes, and you'll see only the scenes that changed. Then press Send.

frames.title: Quick check: a phrase that's flagged
frames.question: In another plan's video, fresh eyes flag the phrase “stage map”, and its author thinks it's clear. What happens before the review page opens?
frames.explain: Every finding is answered before the page opens, fixed, given a meaning, or kept with the reason; the build won't pass one left unanswered.

options.label: Nothing: it opens as it is
The author answers it: fixed, a meaning, or kept with the reason
The build waits for you to decide

frames.narration: Quick check. Fresh eyes flag “stage map” in another video, and its author thinks it's clear. What happens before the review page opens?

frames.title: How a review arrives
frames.narration: Your review reaches the agent one of three ways. Send, on your machine. Send on a hosted page: the review page as a link you open anywhere, Claude only. Or a download you hand it.

frames.title: Who picks it up
frames.narration: Sent on your machine, the review server keeps it in the inbox and hands it on once: to a waiting session; else it starts the headless run, your agent alone in the sandbox, a fence keeping its writes in your repo; else it waits for your next session.

frames.title: Filed once, and on record
frames.narration: `reel record` files the review and adds each answer, with an id like D-264, to the decision log. The log keeps everything, but little of it binds a plan. Of 309, only 65 are rules: your answers in force. The agent's choices are history, back only when a change rewrites their code. And `reel fold` drafts a part's rules as one spec section; once you approve it, plans cite that instead.

frames.title: Only what your words touched
frames.narration: Then the agent revises. Approved: your comments go into `plan.md`, no new video. Changes requested: only the steps your words touched are rewritten, plan-diff marks the scenes that changed, and the player plays just those.

frames.title: Quick check: does it lead somewhere?
frames.question: You pause on a scene with a table, and move your pointer over it. How do you know the table leads to the guide?
frames.explain: A thing that leads to the guide stays quiet: a faint arrow when paused, and on hover a thin ring and “More in the guide”.

options.label: A black tab is drawn on it
A thin ring, and “More in the guide”
Nothing: you open Terms

frames.narration: Quick check. Paused on a scene, your pointer over its table: how do you know the table leads to the guide?

frames.title: Every choice, written down
frames.narration: Once you approve, the agent builds the plan. Each choice the plan didn't cover is a row in `walkthrough.md`, with a label when you might want to look: visible, hard-to-undo, or close. At a step's fifth choice, the agent stops and asks you instead: that step waits, with a question in `plan.md`.

frames.title: A second agent checks
frames.narration: Then the code check: a second agent, new to the work, reads the code against the plan and your decisions. `reel audit` fails until every finding is answered.

frames.title: The change, running
frames.narration: The walkthrough video shows each change running, the real page or a real run, before and after, in about two minutes, with its own guide.

frames.title: What pauses it
frames.narration: `reel stops` decides what pauses it: an off-plan change, where the agent strayed from the plan; a choice labelled visible or hard-to-undo; and one sharing a label with a recent late fix: something a review let through, changed later.

frames.title: A pause, and the list
frames.narration: A pause shows the choice running, with Accept and Flag. Every other choice is on one list at the end, each with a Flag.

frames.title: What was built, and the fix
frames.narration: Under it, the guide's Built side shows what changed, with the real runs. Finish asks again: anything you'd change? Flag a choice, and the agent fixes the code and its row.

frames.title: Quick check: sent at night
frames.question: In a repo set up for Claude Code (`reel init --agent claude`), you press Send at 11 pm, and no agent session is open. What happens to your review?
frames.explain: With no session waiting, the review server starts the headless run on it, inside the sandbox.

options.label: It's lost
It waits for your next session
The headless run starts on it, in the sandbox

frames.narration: Quick check. In a repo set up for Claude Code, you press Send at eleven at night, with no session open. What happens to your review?

frames.title: All of it, as text
frames.narration: The record is text in your repo, under `.reelplanning/`: the spec, the parts, the glossary, the decision log, and each plan's `plan.md`, reviews, `walkthrough.md` and video sources. The inbox stays on your machine; guides and video files are built again, never committed. This repo's own older plans still hold theirs, until its public history leaves them out.

frames.title: This video, kept current
frames.narration: This video is made from three of those files: `spec.md`; `system.json`, the parts of the system and how they connect; and the glossary, each word with a scene. When they change, spec-diff names the scenes to rebuild. system-review sorts each comment on it: fix the video, a small change, or a new plan. This video has no guide yet: `spec.md` holds the rest.

frames.title: What your reviews teach
frames.narration: Your reviews teach it too: `reel status` ends with the memory, lines worked out from the log and your reviews, like how often you take the recommendation. When evidence piles up, a retro proposes skill edits.

frames.title: Explain first
frames.narration: Not ready to plan? `reelplanning explain` makes an explainer: a video of something already there, every fact from a named source. It ends with Done, Explain more, or Plan this.

frames.title: More people
frames.narration: With more people, a big pull request gets its own walkthrough video, on a branch of its own, and the maintainer's review is the one that counts.

frames.title: reelplanning, in one picture
frames.narration: That's reelplanning: a plan you watch and answer, a build you watch and accept, and a record that keeps everything. Install it, ask your agent for a plan, and watch.

termMeanings.plan.md: the file a plan is written in: its problem, its steps and its questions for you
termMeanings.walkthrough.md: the file the agent writes as it builds: what landed in each step, and each choice it made on its own
termMeanings.spec.md: the project's description of itself, in plain prose: what it is for, its parts and its rules
termMeanings.system.json: the project's parts and how they connect, as data
termMeanings.interface: what a step adds that you use: a command and its flags, a file's fields, what a page shows
termMeanings.hyperframes: the video framework that draws each scene as an HTML page and renders the video
termMeanings.maintainer: a person who decides what goes into a repo
termMeanings.author: the agent that made a video
termMeanings.glossary: the project's list of words, one name per thing, each with its meaning
termMeanings.pr-check: the command that says where a pull request stands: waiting on its video, on a review, or ready to merge
termMeanings.case: one kind of input or situation a step handles, with a real example
termMeanings.reel-intake: the command that files a review that came as a row of a hosted page: it checks the row, then records it like any other
termMeanings.the list: the walkthrough video's last scene: every choice that doesn't pause, one line each, with its own Flag
termMeanings.reel fold: the command that gathers a part's many rules into one section of spec.md, once the owner says yes
termMeanings.past choice: a choice the agent made on its own in an earlier build, kept in its walkthrough.md
termMeanings.in force: still binding on later plans: not replaced by a later answer
termMeanings.cite: name a decision by its id, or the spec.md section it is folded into, in the plan's list of the decisions it keeps
termMeanings.pipeline: the third level, all of reelplanning: your answers kept as decisions that later plans are checked against, every review kept, walkthrough videos and the system video

left.what: scene 12 · "26 in force": "in force" has a meaning, but the video has not yet said that your answers are kept as numbered decisions, so I cannot tell where the 26 come from. left.what: scene 28 · "an id" / "D-264": I guess D-264 is one decision-log entry, with the question it answered in decisions.md. left.what: scene 28 · "a plan touching the player cites all 26 of its rules" then "reel fold player": the 26 here matches scene 12, but the video never says why citing 26 ids is a problem or why folding helps (too long? hard to read?). I would need that to see the point. "player" as the argument of the command is only implied to be a part.

left.what: scene 28 · "spec.md#rules-player": "spec.md" is defined, but the "#rules-player" part is never explained. I guess it is a section anchor. "you approve": how and where do I approve a fold (a review? a command?) is not shown.
